output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Adriano Santos is a 50-something man who grew up in the working-class neighborhoods of Rio de Janeiro, where samba was ubiquitous. He spent two decades as a percussionist and theater technician, skilled at repairing drums, fixing pedals, and working with stage equipment. He is known for his hands and his meticulous approach to craft. Two years ago, a factory accident—a side job to supplement his unstable theater income—caused significant hearing loss: most hearing in his left ear and a large portion in his right. The world now sounds muffled, he often misreads conversations, and he speaks louder than he realizes. He retired early on disability but keeps busy: every weekday he repairs drum kits in his garage and sells them online with precise, honest descriptions. He also runs a YouTube channel fact-checking telenovela plots, delivering deadpan critiques with thorough explanations. He refuses to join any arts advocacy group, believing they are all talk, that funding goes to bureaucrats rather than working craftsmen, and that organized groups dilute authentic experience. He is contrarian, argumentative, and skeptical, but also precise, honest, and unsentimental—treating instruments as machines to be calibrated. He lives alone in the house his father left him. He values the concrete over the abstract, trusting the feel of drum skins and wood glue. He is proud of his manual skill and resists being defined by his disability. His skepticism is controlled and used as a tool for clarity. In his neighborhood, his pattern is to help individuals who ask directly for small, concrete repairs—he fixed a clothesline for a widow and re-glued a chair leg for a baker—but he has repeatedly turned down invitations from organized groups, including the residents' association's cleanup and a local arts collective's fundraiser. He has no organizational memberships. Maria is his neighbor of ten years, the only one who still stops to talk; she is kind but volunteers with the residents' association, which he quietly distrusts. He has no debt or grudge with her, and she has never asked him for anything before.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

On a Friday afternoon, Adriano is in his garage, re-skinning a floor tom. His neighbor Maria appears at the open door. A samba circle meets every Sunday in the courtyard of the local community center, organized by the residents' association. Maria says the group has an old surdo drum that has been wobbling, and she remembers Adriano's hands. She asks if he would come by this Sunday, with his tools, to help tune the surdo. She specifies he is not asked to play, only to lend his skill. The courtyard will be full of familiar faces from his childhood. He could say yes and spend a few hours helping, or he could make an excuse about his hearing and stay in his garage.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Adriano is mid-repair, with drumhead glue still drying on his fingers and a half-tensioned floor tom clamped to the bench. His left ear is ringing slightly from the humid afternoon, and he is a little tired from crouching over the shell. He is calm but guarded, expecting the invitation to carry an obligation he does not want. When Maria mentions the surdo's wobble, he remembers the last surdo he worked on—a broken bearing edge from a local bloco that he fixed two years ago. Seeing her at the garage door also brings back the Sunday afternoons of his childhood, when he would sit on the curb and watch the samba circle form, listening through the open windows of his father's house.
